Let $Q(z) = zP(z) - 1$. Since $P$ has degree $m$, $Q$ is a polynomial of degree $m + 1$, so it has exactly $m + 1$ roots (counting multiplicity) in $\mathbb{C}$.

**Applying Rouché's Theorem.** On the unit circle $|z| = 1$, the hypothesis gives:
$$|Q(z)| = |zP(z) - 1| < 1 = |(-1)|.$$

Compare $Q(z) = zP(z) - 1$ with the constant function $g(z) = -1$ on $|z| = 1$. We have $|Q(z)| < |g(z)|$ on the boundary. By Rouché's theorem, $Q(z)$ and $g(z) = -1$ have the same number of zeros inside the open unit disc $|z| < 1$.

Since $g(z) = -1$ has **no zeros**, $Q(z) = zP(z) - 1$ also has **no zeros** inside $|z| < 1$.

**No zeros on the boundary.** On $|z| = 1$, we have $|Q(z)| < 1 < \infty$, and in particular $|Q(z)| < 1$ means $Q(z) \neq 0$ (since $Q(z) = 0$ would give $|Q(z)| = 0$, but more directly, $|Q(z)|<1$ rules out $Q(z)=0$). So there are no roots on the unit circle $|z| = 1$.

**Conclusion.** The polynomial $Q(z) = zP(z) - 1$ has $m + 1$ roots total, none of which lie inside the open unit disc or on the unit circle. Therefore all $m + 1$ roots lie **outside** the closed unit disc $|z| \leq 1$.
